candidates.title: NetOpsTraceBench: a workflow-centered benchmark measuring intent→config traces, validator interaction, and rollback safety
candidates.research_question: Can a publicly reproducible, workflow-centered benchmark that records multi-step agent traces, validator interactions, and rollback events produce operationally meaningful metrics that distinguish plain LLM generation from verifier-assisted workflows in NetOps tasks?
hypotheses: A composite trace-level safety metric (validator-pass rate weighted by rollback frequency and simulated-availability impact) will be significantly higher for verifier-assisted pipelines than for one-shot LLM generation.
Per-task trace metrics will reveal systematic failure modes (e.g., semantic unit errors, missing dependencies) not captured by single-output correctness measures.
Benchmark-derived differences between methods will be robust across at least two simulated network topologies (edge vs. core).
candidates.proposed_design: Assemble a public dataset of 1,200 natural-language operator intents mapped to canonical multi-device configuration sequences and expected execution-ground-truth (reachability and ACL effects). Use two LLM-driven pipelines: (A) one-shot NL→config; (B) generate–validate–repair with an automated verifier and targeted repair prompts. Execute generated configs in Mininet-based emulators and record full agent traces (prompts, model outputs, verifier feedback, repairs) and simulated telemetry. Define and compute a composite safety score combining validator-pass rate, attempted rollback events, and simulated-availability impact. Release dataset, verifiers (parsers), and trace schema.
candidates.expected_data: For each of 1,200 tasks: original intent, baseline LLM config, verifier-assisted final config, verifier pass/fail logs, number of repair iterations, simulated telemetry (ping/flow results), rollback occurrences, time-to-repair, and human-readable failure labels. Aggregate per-method distributions of composite safety score and component metrics.
candidates.primary_outcome: Difference in mean composite safety score between one-shot LLM and verifier-assisted pipeline across tasks; effect size and 95% CI.
candidates.analysis_outline: Predefine primary comparison as paired test across tasks; use Wilcoxon signed-rank test (nonparametric) and paired t-test for effect-size estimate; compute bootstrapped 95% CIs for composite score difference. Secondary analyses: breakdown by failure-mode category, topology type (edge/core), and repair-iteration counts. Report false-negative and false-positive rates for validator judgments against execution-ground-truth. Provide per-task trace exemplars.
risks: Emulator fidelity may not reflect production failure modes, biasing metric applicability.
Constructed intent→config mappings may encode researcher bias and not cover rare real-world policy semantics.
Validator implementation errors could conflate verifier failures with model failures.
Dataset release may expose sensitive operator templates if sourced inadequately; ensure synthetic/consented examples.

candidates.title: Cross-vendor scaling of verifier-assisted NL→config pipelines
candidates.research_question: Does integrating vendor-specific parsers and verifiers with an LLM-based generation pipeline maintain or improve semantic-correctness (validator pass rate) across heterogeneous vendor syntaxes compared to a vendor-agnostic baseline?
hypotheses: A vendor-aware verifier-assisted pipeline will yield a higher validator-pass rate than a vendor-agnostic one across at least three vendor syntaxes (e.g., Cisco IOS, Juniper Junos, Arista EOS).
Improvements will persist after controlling for configuration length and task complexity (i.e., not solely due to simpler vendor formats).
Parser/verifier coverage gaps will account for a majority of residual semantic failures after enabling verifier-assisted repair.
candidates.proposed_design: Curate 900 NL→config tasks evenly split across three representative vendor syntaxes with matched intent complexity. Implement two pipelines: (1) vendor-agnostic LLM prompts producing configs with no vendor checks; (2) LLM with vendor-specific parsing and verifier modules that return structured errors and drive iterative repairs. Validate outputs with vendor-parsers and execute in per-vendor emulators or syntactic validators; collect validator pass/fail, semantic error types, repair iterations, and final execution checks (where emulator allows). Evaluate per-vendor performance and pooled performance; release parsers and verifier specifications.
candidates.expected_data: Per-task records including vendor, intent, initial LLM output, verifier errors, repair logs, final validator pass/fail, categorized semantic error types (syntax, policy, dependency), and execution-checks where available. Summary tables of pass rates by vendor and complexity strata.
candidates.primary_outcome: Increase in validator-pass rate for vendor-aware verifier-assisted pipeline versus vendor-agnostic baseline (paired per-task), with p-value and effect size.
candidates.analysis_outline: Primary analysis: mixed-effects logistic regression with task as random effect and fixed effects for pipeline, vendor, and complexity, testing pipeline coefficient. Secondary: per-vendor paired comparisons (McNemar or paired-proportion tests), analysis of residual failure causes (percentage attributable to parser gaps). Report confidence intervals and adjust for multiple comparisons (Benjamini–Hochberg).
risks: Vendor parsers/verifiers may be incomplete, producing false failure attributions.
Emulator coverage may differ by vendor, limiting execution-grounded validation for some syntaxes.
Licensing or proprietary syntax edge cases could be omitted, reducing external validity.
LLM hallucinations may generate superficially plausible but semantically incorrect constructs that parsers fail to flag.

candidates.title: Provenance-linked runtime detection of hallucination and policy violations in agentic NetOps
candidates.research_question: Can lightweight provenance features linking LLM outputs to retrieval/document sources improve automated detection of hallucinated or policy-violating NetOps proposals compared to output-only heuristics?
hypotheses: Incorporating provenance-derived features (source-match score, citation density, retrieval-recall) into a detector will significantly improve AUC for identifying hallucinated or policy-violating proposals versus detectors using only text-derived features.
Provenance features will particularly reduce false negatives for hallucinations that introduce fabricated device identifiers or non-existent policies.
Adversarially crafted prompts reduce detector performance, but provenance-enhanced detectors degrade less than text-only baselines under the same adversary budget.
candidates.proposed_design: Construct a labeled corpus (≈2,000 examples) of LLM-generated NetOps proposals: grounded outputs, hallucinated outputs, and explicit policy-violating proposals. For each output, record retrieval provenance (documents/sections used), link strength metrics (token overlap, retrieval score), and text features. Train multiple classifiers: baseline (text features), provenance-enhanced, and adversarial-robustified provenance-enhanced. Evaluate detection AUC, precision/recall, and under simulated adversarial prompts (prompt-injection patterns).
candidates.expected_data: For each example: intent, LLM output, provenance links (doc IDs, retrieval scores), label (grounded/hallucinated/policy-violation), classifier predictions, and adversarial perturbation logs. Aggregated classifier metrics (AUC, precision@k) and robustness curves under adversarial strength.
candidates.primary_outcome: Increase in detection AUC (provenance-enhanced vs text-only) on held-out test set with bootstrapped 95% CI.
candidates.analysis_outline: Train/test splits fixed with stratification; compare ROC AUCs using DeLong's test. Report precision/recall at operational thresholds and calibration plots. For adversarial evaluation, compute AUC as adversary budget varies and report degradation slopes. Provide error analysis with exemplar failures and confusion matrices.
risks: Adversarial actors may adapt to provenance signals, reducing long-term detector efficacy.
False positives could unnecessarily block safe operational changes, increasing operator workload.
Provenance instrumentation adds latency and storage cost to agentic workflows.
Labeled hallucination/policy-violation datasets may be hard to curate without domain expert input; synthetic labeling risks bias.

candidates.title: Simulated HITL oversight policies: balancing safety and operator burden in reversible NetOps tasks
candidates.research_question: Which human-in-the-loop oversight patterns (automatic, canary-with-auto-rollback, human-approval-for-high-risk) optimize the trade-off between severe incident reduction and operator intervention burden for reversible NetOps changes in simulated operations?
hypotheses: A tiered oversight policy that routes low-risk changes to automated canaries and high-risk changes to human approval will reduce severe simulated incidents more than a fully automated policy while increasing operator interventions less than a universal human-approval policy.
Canary-with-auto-rollback will catch a majority of severe semantic failures with lower operator burden than mandatory human approval.
Relative policy performance will depend on reversibility: for highly reversible changes, automated canary policies approach human-approval safety with substantially fewer interventions.
candidates.proposed_design: Simulate 1,500 NetOps change tasks labeled with risk and reversibility tiers and mapped to expected failure impact. Implement three oversight policies in the simulation: (A) fully automated commit, (B) canary execution with automated rollback and telemetry-based gating, (C) risk-tiered human-approval (simulated operator model) for high-risk tasks. Use LLM-generated proposals with injected realistic failure rates (based on prior literature). Measure severe-incident rate, number of human interventions (simulated approvals), mean time-to-recovery, and availability impact. Conduct sensitivity analysis by varying LLM base failure rates and canary detection sensitivity.
candidates.expected_data: Per-simulated-task records: risk tier, reversibility flag, chosen oversight action, canary telemetry outcome, rollback events, whether simulated severe incident occurred, simulated operator interaction timestamps and counts. Aggregated metrics: severe-incident rate, interventions per 100 tasks, availability loss, and time-to-recovery.
candidates.primary_outcome: Policy trade-off curve: severe incidents prevented per additional human intervention comparing policies, reported with 95% CIs; identification of Pareto-optimal policy under simulated cost model.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compute incident rates and intervention counts per policy; compare policies using Poisson or negative-binomial regression for count outcomes and survival analysis for time-to-recovery. Produce cost–benefit curves parameterized by operator cost and incident cost; run sensitivity sweeps over LLM failure-rate and canary sensitivity. Report threshold regions where each policy is optimal.
risks: Simulated operator model may not capture real human decision patterns, limiting external validity.
Parametric assumptions about LLM failure rates could bias policy recommendations.
Canary detectors in simulation may overestimate real-world detection fidelity.
No-live-human trials may reduce confidence in operational acceptability of recommended policies.
